articles.title: AI Isn’t Replacing Creativity
articles.excerpt: It is changing who gets to create, how quickly ideas become real, and what creative leadership means next.
articles.body:
Every few months, the same question returns: is AI going to replace creativity? I think that question is too small.

It assumes creativity is the act of producing an image, writing a paragraph, generating a video, designing a screen or creating an animation. It is not. Those are outputs.

Creativity starts earlier: recognising something that does not exist yet; framing a problem differently; connecting unrelated ideas; understanding people; making choices under uncertainty; establishing a point of view; and turning an abstract possibility into something another person can experience.

AI can generate. That does not mean it knows what is worth generating.

I have spent much of my career working at the intersection of design, animation, immersive technology, physical environments, brand systems and emerging technology. One thing has remained consistent: the difficult part is rarely producing the thing. The difficult part is deciding what the thing should be.

Creative technology has always changed production. Digital compositing changed filmmaking. 3D changed visualisation. Motion graphics changed communication. Real-time engines changed interactive experiences. XR changed the relationship between physical and digital environments.

AI is another major shift in that progression. But reducing the cost of production is not the same as reducing the need for creative thinking.

AI can help teams explore visual directions, generate early concepts, create variations, analyse information, accelerate research, prototype interactions, produce copy, organise references and automate repetitive production tasks.

That is significant. But when everyone can produce more, production itself becomes less valuable as a differentiator. The question changes from “Can we make it?” to “Should we make it this way — and why should anyone care?”

As generation becomes abundant, creative value shifts toward intention, direction, curation and judgment.

Production becomes faster. The value of deciding which possibility deserves to survive increases.

For decades, creative industries were constrained by expensive equipment, specialist software, large teams, long timelines, technical expertise, post-production and fabrication. The distance between an idea and a finished artefact could be enormous.

AI compresses that distance. A person can now move from thought to exploration, variation and prototype in dramatically less time. The bottleneck moves — first to taste, then judgment, context, meaning and ultimately responsibility.

The machine can increase the number of possibilities. The creative leader decides which possibilities deserve to survive.

“Create a futuristic corporate experience” is a prompt. It describes a category. “Create an environment where a senior executive understands the company’s transformation strategy within five minutes without feeling like they are being presented with a technology demonstration” is closer to creative direction.

Now the problem has an audience, a context, a desired outcome, a time constraint, an emotional requirement and a communication objective. The machine can help explore the solution, but someone still has to define the problem.

A prompt can describe what to generate. Creative direction defines why it should exist.

Many AI-generated experiences begin to look strangely similar: polished, beautiful, technically impressive and forgettable. The same cinematic lighting, floating objects, future aesthetic and visual shorthand.

A creative identity cannot simply be assembled from patterns. A strong point of view often comes from constraints, lived experience, culture, observation, unexpected references and knowing what not to do.

Taste is not just preference. It is recognising the difference between possible and appropriate; impressive and effective; new and necessary; beautiful and meaningful; technically possible and humanly useful.

AI expands the first side of those comparisons. Creative leadership must increasingly protect the second.

Generation becomes abundant. Distinction becomes scarce — and therefore valuable.

Generation

Differentiation

As generation gets easier, the small decisions that create meaningful difference become more important.

The old model was brief, concept, team, production, review and delivery. The AI-era model is increasingly problem, human insight, creative direction, AI exploration, selection, experience and learning.

Less time needs to be spent manually controlling every production step. More time can be spent defining problems, establishing creative principles, setting quality thresholds, connecting disciplines, protecting the human experience and making strategic trade-offs.

Creative leadership moves upstream.

In XR, VR, interactive environments and experience centres, a visitor does not necessarily care that an experience uses projection, sensors, real-time graphics, spatial interfaces or automation. They care about what those things allow them to understand, feel or do.

An AI model is not the experience. A generated image is not the idea. A chatbot is not the strategy. They are mechanisms. The creative challenge is determining what those mechanisms should enable.

Do not move from prompt to approval. Preserve the question inside the creative process.

Question the output, assumption, direction and obvious answer. That is creative thinking.

Teams can now explore five, twenty or fifty directions before deciding which one deserves development. Experimentation becomes cheaper. When experimentation becomes cheaper, creative teams can take more intellectual risks.

AI should not only help us make existing work faster. It should help us explore ideas we previously could not afford to explore.

But speed can also destroy thinking. When production becomes extremely fast, teams can start mistaking speed for progress. The machine keeps moving while the idea does not.

Sometimes the best next step is not another generation. It is a question: What are we actually trying to say? Why does this need to exist? Who is this for? What if we removed it?

The human layer is not a decorative review step. It establishes the direction of the system.

Human

AI

Together: more possibilities, better experimentation, faster iteration, stronger decisions and more meaningful experiences.

If everything can be created, restraint becomes a creative skill. No to another animation. No to another interaction. No to another screen, feature or AI-generated variation. No because the experience is already communicating clearly.

That judgment is not anti-technology. It is responsible creativity. It is also why originality matters more when visual impressiveness is easy to create.

Case study connection

Orange Business demonstrates creative leadership across physical, digital and interactive systems — designed around a coherent executive journey.

Do not start with “How can we use AI?” Start with “Where does AI create meaningful leverage?” Sometimes AI belongs in ideation, research, visual exploration, production or personalisation. Sometimes it belongs nowhere.

The mature question is not whether a project contains AI. It is whether AI improves the outcome.

Framework 06

Before introducing AI into a creative workflow, test whether it creates genuine leverage. Select each stage to inspect the decision.

Start with the capability. Name what the tool can genuinely help a team do — but do not mistake capability for a reason to use it.

Does it solve a real creative problem? If it only accelerates output while weakening the concept, reconsider its role.

Does it expand exploration? Meaningful value appears when a team can investigate possibilities that would otherwise remain unexplored.

Does it improve the experience? The audience should benefit — not only the production team.

Does a human still own the decision? Someone must remain accountable for the creative choice and the experience it produces.

Does the result have a point of view? If it could have been produced by anyone using the same tool, it needs another layer of thinking.

articles.title: Technology Should Feel Human
articles.excerpt: The best technology does not make people feel like they are using technology. It makes them feel capable, understood and connected.
articles.body:
Artificial intelligence can generate, analyse and interpret information at extraordinary speed. Virtual reality can place people inside simulated environments. Spatial computing can turn the environment around us into an interface.

Technology is getting remarkably sophisticated. But sophistication can also create the opposite of a better experience: more features, more interfaces, more choices, more notifications and more complexity.

That leads to a more important question than “How advanced is the technology?”: How human does the experience feel?

An AI product can be intelligent but confusing. A VR experience can be immersive but uncomfortable. An interactive installation can be visually impressive but provide no meaningful reason to interact. A digital product can have hundreds of features while hiding the one feature someone needs.

The technology works. The experience does not. The designer’s responsibility is not to expose technological capability. It is to translate capability into human value.

With AI, it is tempting to ask what it can generate. With VR, what it can simulate. With AR, what it can overlay. These are useful questions, but they should come later.

The first questions are: Who is experiencing this? What are they trying to achieve? What do they struggle with? What should become easier, possible, understandable or meaningful?

Technology should be selected because it improves the human outcome — not because it is new.

Start with the human outcome. Let technology become the enabler.

Technology becomes noticeable when navigation is confusing, a gesture is not recognised, an interaction behaves unexpectedly, an AI response is unclear or an installation requires instructions longer than the experience itself.

At that point, the person stops experiencing the intended outcome. They start experiencing the technology. The interface has become the problem.

You do not need a manual or someone standing beside you explaining it. You see an invitation, interact, the system responds, you understand what happened, and you continue. Enormous technical complexity can sit beneath that sequence without becoming the user’s burden.

Immersive environments remove familiar boundaries. People can look around, move, explore, interact, listen, reach and choose. The experience can respond to them. That creates extraordinary possibilities — and questions about attention, interaction, recovery, information load and behaviour.

A person can feel completely present inside a virtual environment and still have a poor experience. The better question is: What does their sense of presence allow them to do?

If immersion helps someone understand a complex system, safely practise a dangerous situation or access a perspective they could not otherwise experience, it has purpose. The technology becomes valuable because it changes human possibility.

Good experience design does not eliminate complexity. It prevents unnecessary complexity from reaching the person.

AI can generate responses, adapt, interpret, recommend, predict and personalise. That can make experiences feel natural, but it can also introduce uncertainty. If a system behaves differently each time, people need enough understanding to know what to expect.

Human-centred AI is not about making systems pretend to be human. It is about intent, context, control, transparency, feedback, error recovery, accessibility, trust and responsibility.

Technology amplifies capability, information and connection. Experience design gives those possibilities direction.

The Orange Business Executive Briefing Center brought together physical space, brand experience, digital content, interactive media, video, VR and environmental technology. Registration, synchronisation, personalised greetings, automation and coordination happened behind the scenes.

From the outside, those can appear to be separate technology features. For the visitor, they needed to feel like one coherent, responsive journey. The visitor should never need to understand the technology stack.

Case study

See how physical space, content, interaction, VR and environmental technology came together around one clear human journey.

People do not experience products under laboratory conditions. They use them while distracted, tired, in a hurry, unfamiliar with the environment, helping someone else or under pressure.

A human-centred experience accounts for people who forget, make mistakes, change their minds, get interrupted and approach problems differently. Design not only for the ideal interaction, but for mistakes, uncertainty, recovery and variation.

Before introducing emerging technology, evaluate the human problem — not simply the technical possibility.

Framework 04

Choose each step to test whether a new technology should earn a place in the experience.

Does it solve a real human problem? If no meaningful problem exists, reconsider the technology.

Does the person understand what is happening? Technical detail can stay hidden, but the experience needs to make sense.

Does the person feel in control? People should understand their choices and the consequences of their actions.

Does it create meaningful capability? Can the person now do something better, faster, safer, deeper or differently?

Does it create a better human experience? If the technology makes the journey harder, it has not earned its place.

articles.title: Why Enterprise Experiences Fail
articles.excerpt: The problem is rarely a lack of technology. It is usually the distance between what an organisation intends and what people actually experience.
articles.body:
Enterprise experiences rarely fail because someone could not build them. The technology usually works. The screens turn on. The content loads. The application responds. The installation launches. And yet something feels wrong.

People do not understand it. Teams do not adopt it. The story changes from one touchpoint to another. Stakeholders disagree about what matters. Technology becomes more complicated than the problem it was meant to solve.

After working across creative, brand, immersive technology, physical environments, digital experiences and multidisciplinary teams, I have become convinced that enterprise experience is not a single-discipline problem. It is a connection problem.

A person can encounter an organisation through a website, email, sales presentation, mobile application, physical office, showroom, support interaction, product demonstration, event, training environment, service portal or a conversation with a person. Each may have been made by a different team, vendor, department, technology stack and timeline.

The person does not care who owns which component. They experience one organisation.

Internal organisational structure rarely matches external human experience. The larger the gap, the more fragmented the journey can feel.

A project can launch on time, meet requirements, pass QA, satisfy a stakeholder and still create a poor overall experience. It may have optimised the project rather than the journey.

Project thinking asks, “Did we deliver what was requested?” Experience thinking asks, “Did the person get what they needed?” Those are not always the same question.

“Digitally transform the customer journey.” “Create an immersive experience.” “Build an innovation centre.” “Develop an AI-powered platform.” These requests can be ambitious without explaining what a person needs to understand, do, feel or decide.

The missing layer is usually the human outcome. What should become easier? What should they remember? What behaviour should become possible? Without those answers, a team can end up designing the requested artefact instead of solving the problem underneath it.

The strategic creative work happens in the bridge between business intent and what a person actually needs.

AI, VR, AR, spatial computing, interactive displays, digital twins, sensors and automation can all be useful. But the question “Where can we put it?” is weaker than the question, “What experience could not exist—or work as well—without it?”

Every technology needs a job. It might explain, demonstrate, personalise, connect, simulate, enable, automate or reveal. If nobody can describe that job in one sentence, it deserves another conversation.

One team designs the website. Another designs the app. Another creates the showroom, presentation, campaign or VR experience. Each team can produce excellent work; still, the experience can feel inconsistent because each optimised a touchpoint while nobody owned the journey.

Touchpoints are supporting components. A journey gives them sequence, relevance and a shared point of view.

Enterprise work brings together leadership, marketing, IT, operations, sales, legal, security, procurement, product, regional teams, agencies and vendors. Their perspectives are legitimate. But when every stakeholder has equal authority over every decision, the work becomes an accumulation of compromises: safe, generic, overloaded and unclear.

Good collaboration means that everyone knows what they own, influence and advise on—and who makes the final decision when the disciplines disagree.

Business, human and technology value must remain connected. Experience is where they become coherent.

Enterprise environments can include content systems, registration, displays, networks, sensors, automation, databases, media servers, VR hardware, physical controls, analytics and integrations. A visitor does not need to understand that stack. They need to know where they are, what is happening, what they can do and why it matters.

A sophisticated system can produce a simple experience. That is often the point.

The more complicated the system underneath, the more important the translation layer becomes.

The people approving a project and the people using it are usually different audiences. The executive approving a platform is not necessarily the customer. The IT leader approving training is not necessarily the trainee. Both perspectives matter, but they ask different questions.

A successful enterprise project has to survive governance and serve the person without confusing those needs.

When the platform is designed, the screens installed and the space built before someone asks what will go on it, the experience is already constrained. Narrative should influence spatial layout, interaction, hierarchy, screen placement, motion, pacing, navigation and technology choices.

Technology determines what can happen. Content determines what should happen. Design determines how it is experienced. Strategy determines why it matters.

Sequential process is efficient only when the central problem is already understood. In enterprise experience work, strategy, experience, design, content and technology need early cross-disciplinary decisions, then continuous feedback.

Every discipline remains distinct. Every discipline still understands the experience it is contributing to.

The website team owns the website. The technology vendor owns the installation. The brand team owns the guidelines. The content team owns the video. The architect owns the space. And the customer owns the confusion.

Enterprise experience needs an empowered person or team to maintain the experience point of view across disciplines—not to control every detail, but to protect coherence.

Numbers of screens, visitors, interactions, features or assets are useful, but not sufficient. Better questions are: Did people understand? Did the experience reduce friction? Did it create confidence? Did behaviour change? Did it support the objective?

Measurement should follow the intended human outcome—not only the easiest available count.

Someone updates the content, maintains the hardware, handles exceptions, manages data, trains staff, resets the system and responds when something breaks. If that operational layer is not designed, even a beautiful visitor experience gradually degrades.

The audience should experience the frontstage. The organisation must be able to sustain the backstage.

Case study / Orange Business

The New Executive Briefing Center in Mumbai connected physical space, brand, interactive content, video, VR, registration, personalised communication, screens, automation and coordination across teams. Its lesson was clear: a complex experience becomes coherent only when each component understands its role in the same journey.

That same translation is visible in the BPCL Palakkad experience, where complex industrial information needed to become visual storytelling, spatial communication and accessible understanding—not simply more information on a wall.

I worked directly with the Major on a daily basis, collaborating on requirements, progress, feedback and iterations.
I worked with the Colonel on a weekly basis for reviews, alignment, direction and feedback.
At senior review level, I coordinated the work through Brigadier-level approval.
This placed me directly between the Army stakeholders, the experience strategy and the team responsible for bringing the training environment to life.

I was not handed a brief and asked to produce visuals. The work was to translate what the Army needed into an immersive training experience, take that experience back to the stakeholders for review, and coordinate the people and work required to deliver it.
Highlighted stages are where I led directly. Stakeholder relationships describe project collaboration, review and approval — not military command.

sections.heading: Before the battlefield, there is a learning curve.
paragraphs: Complex operational training requires more than information. Personnel need an environment in which they can learn, practise, repeat and demonstrate their understanding before moving into physical training.

The opportunity was to create an immersive digital layer that could sit between learning and physical training — allowing trainees to experience the training environment through VR while giving instructors visibility into the process.

sections.heading: 15 stations. One connected training environment.
paragraphs: The physical foundation of the experience was a dedicated training room equipped with 15 high-end computer stations for VR-based training.
Each trainee could participate in an individual immersive session while a high-end central display gave the trainer a consolidated view of what trainees were doing inside their VR environments.
The result was not simply a room full of individual VR experiences. It was a connected training environment where individual immersion and centralised instruction existed together.
15 high-end computer stations — one trainee, one individual VR session per station.
Dedicated training room — set up for Army personnel as a purpose-built training space.
High-end central display — the trainer's consolidated view of trainee activity.
Two platforms — T-70 and T-90 experiences within one training framework.

images.alt: The dedicated training room: fifteen high-end computer stations with VR headsets arranged in rows before the large central instructor display

sections.heading: Immersion for the trainee. Visibility for the trainer.
paragraphs: Immersive training can become isolated if the instructor cannot see what is happening inside the experience. This system connected both sides.
Trainees remained immersed in their individual VR sessions, while the trainer retained a centralised view of the training activity through the main display.

This allowed instruction, observation and assessment to remain connected to the immersive experience. The trainer could see what each trainee was doing during their session — not after it — and guide the room accordingly.
Designing for the instructor with the same care as the trainee was one of the most important decisions in the project. It is what turned fifteen private experiences into one training environment.

images.alt: The trainer standing before the large central display, which shows a grid of every trainee's VR session alongside platform and session panels

sections.heading: Observation stayed inside the loop.
paragraphs: Because trainee activity was visible on the central display, the trainer could observe individual sessions, follow progress through the training and bring attention to a specific trainee when needed.
The same visibility carried into assessment: what the trainer observed during practice became the basis for evaluating readiness to qualify.

images.alt: The trainer at the monitoring console reviewing an individual trainee's session on the command view, with the station grid beside it

sections.heading: T-90
paragraphs: Learn inside the machine.
The T-90 was brought into the immersive training environment as part of the digital learning and practice experience.
The goal was to give trainees an immersive environment in which they could engage with the training experience before progressing to the next stage of training.

images.alt: The T-90 in the immersive training environment, framed by the training module panel

sections.heading: T-70
paragraphs: The same immersive training principle.
The T-70 was integrated into the same broader immersive training approach.
Rather than treating each platform as an isolated experience, the project established a consistent digital training framework across the two platforms.

images.alt: The T-70 in the immersive training environment on open terrain, with the training module panel visible

sections.heading: Two platforms. One training logic.
paragraphs: The strength of the experience was not only in recreating individual platforms digitally.

It was in creating a broader training logic that could move personnel through learning, practice and qualification within the immersive environment — the same logic, whichever platform a trainee was working on.

images.alt: Two platforms, one training ecosystem: the T-90 and T-70 shown side by side above a shared strip of training modules

sections.heading: Inside the experience.
paragraphs: For the trainee, the experience was direct and immersive.
VR placed the training environment around the individual, creating a space where learning and practice could happen through active participation rather than observation alone.

images.alt: First-person view from inside the T-90 training environment: the crew position and viewport looking out over mountainous terrain

sections.heading: Individual immersion. Shared visibility.
paragraphs: Each of the fifteen stations ran an individual VR session. What a trainee experienced was theirs alone — but what they were doing was visible to the trainer on the central display. That pairing of individual immersion and centralised visibility is the defining relationship of the ecosystem.

images.alt: A trainee wearing a VR headset at a station, hands on the controls, with the training module on the monitor and the central display in the background

sections.heading: Training became assessable.
paragraphs: The immersive environment also became the setting for qualification testing.
Trainees were not simply experiencing the environment. They were expected to demonstrate their understanding and performance within it.
This introduced an important transition — from an environment in which you learn to one in which you are expected to show what you have learned.

images.alt: Qualification test view from inside the T-90 environment: assessment stages listed on the left, the crew position in the centre, and the qualification panel on the right

sections.heading: What the trainer saw became the decision.
paragraphs: Assessment drew on the same central visibility the trainer used during practice: which trainees had worked through the training, how they had performed inside the environment, and who was ready to qualify.
That is what allowed qualification to be a considered stage rather than a formality.

images.alt: The trainer reviewing a trainee's assessment view on the central display

sections.heading: Qualified.
paragraphs: A defined stage between digital learning and physical training.
Qualification created a defined stage between digital learning and physical training.
The immersive environment could therefore function not only as a training space, but also as a point at which trainees demonstrated their competency before progressing further.

images.alt: A trainee at a station looks up at the screen confirming a qualified result, with the central display in the background

sections.heading: VR didn't replace the battlefield.
paragraphs: It prepared the trainee for the next stage.
The purpose of immersive training was not to replace physical training.
It created a digital preparation and qualification stage before personnel progressed toward physical, battlefield-based training.
Once trainees excelled in the digital training environment, they could progress to the next stage of physical training.

images.alt: Split composition: a trainee in a VR headset with a qualified result on the left, transitioning to a tank crossing real terrain on the right

sections.heading: From immersion to physical training.
paragraphs: The digital environment was one stage of a larger training journey.

After demonstrating competency within the immersive environment, personnel could progress toward physical training. The experience therefore connected two worlds: immersive practice and physical training.

images.alt: Tanks moving across open high-altitude terrain during physical training

sections.heading: A training ecosystem, not a single screen.
paragraphs: At the system level, every part of the facility had a place in one chain — from the fifteen stations to the point at which a trainee progressed to physical training.

images.alt: System architecture overview connecting the trainee stations, the immersive VR environment, the instructor view, assessment and qualification, and progression to physical training

sections.heading: The experience was built around the training.
paragraphs: My role extended beyond the visual layer.

I was involved in shaping the experience and content that trainees encountered inside the immersive environment, translating requirements into a structured training journey and coordinating its development through iteration and stakeholder feedback.

images.alt: Close view of the training content structure on a station monitor beside the vehicle model

sections.heading: Working at the speed of the stakeholder.
paragraphs: Three cadences ran through the whole project. Each one was mine to prepare for, present to and act on.
Working through requirements, reviewing progress, discussing feedback, aligning the experience, resolving issues and driving iterations.
Progress reviews, direction, feedback, alignment and presentation of the evolving work.
Taking the work through senior-level review for Brigadier-level approval.
Direct collaboration → review → alignment → senior approval.

Working directly with Army stakeholders throughout the project meant continuously translating requirements into experience decisions, taking feedback back to the team, iterating the work and presenting the evolving solution for review.
These were project relationships — collaboration, review and approval of the work. They do not describe a military position or command authority.

sections.heading: Led the experience, end to end.
paragraphs: Strategy, direction, content, stakeholders, team and execution — held together across the lifecycle of the project rather than handed off after the concept.
Defined how the immersive experience could support the broader training journey.
Shaped the overall experience, storytelling and creative approach.
Directed how trainees would encounter and move through the digital environment.
Created and shaped the content required for the immersive training experience.
Worked directly with the Major, the Colonel and the Brigadier-level approval process.
Coordinated the team responsible for developing and executing the experience.
Managed feedback, iterations, reviews and alignment.
Stayed involved across the lifecycle rather than handing off the work after strategy or concept development.

sections.heading: Behind every system is a trainee.
paragraphs: The technology was only valuable if it made the training experience understandable, immersive and assessable for the person using it.
The work therefore had to operate at two levels simultaneously: the individual trainee experience, and the instructor's ability to understand and guide that experience.

Individual trainee experiences remained visible to the instructor.
Qualification testing became part of the immersive environment.
Training could move from digital practice toward physical training.
The project connected people, content, technology, instruction and qualification into one training ecosystem.
